title: Build the Minimum-Cost Backbone Network
real_world_story: The company has a list of all links it could lease between its towers, routers and switching centers, each with a monthly lease cost. It must choose a subset of these links that connects every node while paying as little as possible overall.

real_world_connection.input_represents: All candidate links and their lease costs
real_world_connection.output_represents: The minimum total cost to connect every node
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Building a minimum spanning backbone network (spanning tree)

problem_statement: Given N nodes numbered 0 to N-1 and E candidate undirected links with lease costs, find the minimum total cost required to connect all N nodes into a single connected backbone network.
task: Return the total cost of the minimum-cost spanning network. If the network cannot connect all nodes, return -1.
input_format: The first line contains two integers N and E. The next E lines each contain three integers u v w describing a candidate link between nodes u and v with lease cost w.
output_format: Print the minimum total lease cost that connects all nodes, or -1 if they cannot all be connected.

examples.explanation: The cheapest way to connect all nodes uses the links 2-3 (4), 0-3 (5) and 0-1 (10), for a total of 19.

expected_algorithm.name: Kruskal's Algorithm
expected_algorithm.reason: Sorting candidate links by cost and adding the cheapest link that does not create a cycle yields the minimum-cost spanning tree.

hint: Sort all candidate links by lease cost.
Add each candidate in order if it connects two still-unconnected groups.
Use a union-find structure to track which nodes are already connected.
Stop once N - 1 links have been selected.
real_world_takeaway: Kruskal's algorithm lets a communication company build a fully connected backbone at the minimum lease cost by choosing the cheapest non-redundant links.
